title: Unlocking the Retina's Secrets: A Comprehensive Guide to OCT Biomarkers
summary: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) has revolutionized ophthalmic diagnostics, providing unprecedented insight into retinal and choroidal pathology. OCT biomarkers are quantifiable or qualitative features identified on OCT scans that serve as critical indicators of disease activity, progression, and treatment response across a spectrum of ocular conditions. This poster delves deep into the pathophysiology, classification, clinical significance, and management implications of these vital retinal signatures.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: OCT biomarkers are identifiable structural features within retinal and choroidal layers, detected on Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) scans, that correlate with underlying disease processes. They serve as objective, quantifiable, and qualitative indicators for diagnosing, monitoring disease activity, assessing prognosis, and guiding treatment decisions across various retinal pathologies. These markers are crucial for understanding disease pathophysiology and evaluating therapeutic efficacy in real-time.

content.description: OCT biomarkers are central to managing the leading causes of blindness globally. The prevalence of conditions where OCT biomarkers are critical highlights their immense clinical utility. OCT is the gold standard for monitoring these diseases, with adoption rates in ophthalmology clinics exceeding 90% in developed countries.

branches: Vascular Leakage/Dysfunction (e.g., IRF, SRF, PED) → Anti-VEGF related
RPE Dysfunction/Damage (e.g., Drusen, Atrophy, PED) → AMD, CSR
Photoreceptor Degeneration (e.g., EZ/ELM disruption) → AMD, IRD, DR
Inflammation/Exudation (e.g., HRF) → DR, RVO, inflammatory conditions
Ischemia/Neurodegeneration (e.g., DRIL, RNFL/GCC thinning) → DR, RVO, Glaucoma
Vitreoretinal Interface Abnormalities (e.g., VMT, ERM) → Tractional forces
Neovascularization (e.g., CNV, IRMA on OCTA) → Angiogenesis, vascular proliferation

sections.title: 5. Ocular Examination Findings (OCT-Specific)
content: **SD-OCT/SS-OCT**: High-resolution cross-sectional imaging of retinal layers.
**Enhanced Depth Imaging (EDI-OCT)**: Improved visualization of choroid and sub-RPE structures.
**OCT Angiography (OCTA)**: Non-invasive, depth-resolved visualization of retinal and choroidal vasculature, identifying flow abnormalities (e.g., CNV, IRMA, FAZ enlargement).
**Fundus Autofluorescence (FAF) (Complementary)**: RPE health and lipofuscin accumulation, often correlating with geographic atrophy seen on OCT.

sections.title: 6. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **Step 1: Clinical History & Vision Assessment**: Evaluate symptoms (metamorphopsia, vision loss) and VA.
**Step 2: Dilated Fundus Examination**: Rule out other pathologies, assess gross retinal status.
**Step 3: Comprehensive OCT Scan**: Macular cube (e.g., 512x128, 512x512, 200x200), B-scans, en face images. Assess for all relevant biomarkers.
**Step 4: OCT Angiography (OCTA)**: If neovascularization is suspected (CNV, IRMA, FAZ changes).

**Step 5: Fluorescein Angiography (FFA) / Indocyanine Green Angiography (ICGA)**: If OCT/OCTA findings are equivocal or for specific conditions (e.g., PCV, inflammatory CNV). FFA identifies leakage, ICGA for choroidal circulation and polypoidal lesions.
**Step 6: Fundus Photography / Autofluorescence (FAF)**: Document baseline, monitor atrophy and drusen.

rows: nAMD: Subretinal CNV. CSR: RPE detachments, pachychoroid. PCV: Polypoidal lesions on ICGA.
DME/RVO: Microaneurysms, exudates. RAP: Retinal-choroidal anastomosis. Inflammatory: Vitritis, vasculitis.
nAMD: Associated CNV. CSR: Dome-shaped, often without CNV. PCV: 'Notch' sign, polyps on ICGA.
DME, nAMD, RVO (exudates, hemorrhage), RPE migration
DME/RVO: Associated with fluid/edema. RPE migration: Often in atrophic areas.
nAMD: Often overlying CNV or atrophy. IRD: Diffuse or specific patterns (e.g., RP). Macular Edema: Swelling-related stretching/damage.

sections.title: 8. Staging & Grading with OCT Biomarkers
content: **AMD (AREDS Classification)**: Drusen size/area, pigmentary changes, GA, nAMD. OCT quantifies drusen volume, identifies early GA, CNV type.
**Diabetic Retinopathy (ETDRS/DRCR.net)**: Macular edema (CST, IRF, SRF), DRIL, EZ integrity, HRF are key for severity and treatment response.
**Glaucoma**: RNFL thickness, GCC thickness, optic nerve head parameters (cup-to-disc ratio, rim area) are crucial for staging and progression analysis.
**Vitreomacular Interface**: VMT (stage 0-4), ERM (grade 1-3). OCT precisely defines tractional forces and retinal distortion.
**Geographic Atrophy (GA)**: OCT measures RPE atrophy, outer retinal atrophy (ORA), and choroidal atrophy. Quantifies area and progression rate.

sections.title: 9. Management & Treatment Guided by OCT
content: **Step 1: Initial Diagnosis**: OCT identifies active disease (e.g., fluid in nAMD/DME).

**Step 2: Treatment Initiation**: Anti-VEGF therapy (e.g., Aflibercept 2mg, Ranibizumab 0.5mg, Bevacizumab 1.25mg, Brolucizumab 6mg, Faricimab 6mg) for nAMD, DME, RVO macular edema. Dosing frequency (e.g., q4w, q8w, treat-and-extend) is tailored.

**Step 3: Monitoring Treatment Response**: Serial OCT scans (typically monthly) assess fluid resolution (IRF, SRF, PED reduction), HRF changes. Persistence of fluid or new fluid dictates re-treatment or dose adjustment.
**Step 4: Prognostic Indicators**: Poor visual prognosis despite fluid resolution if EZ/ELM disruption or DRIL persists. Progression of GA monitored.
**Step 5: Surgical Intervention**: OCT confirms VMT, ERM, macular hole, guiding vitrectomy for release of traction or hole closure. Pre-op OCT guides surgical approach (e.g., ILM peel).

sections.title: 10. Complications & Prognosis
content: **Persistent Fluid (IRF/SRF)**: Associated with worse long-term visual acuity outcomes, despite treatment.
**EZ/ELM Disruption/Loss**: Indicates irreversible photoreceptor damage, directly correlates with poorer visual prognosis.
**DRIL**: Strong predictor of poor visual recovery in DME and RVO, even after edema resolution.
**Geographic Atrophy (GA)**: Progressive RPE and photoreceptor loss, leading to irreversible vision loss. OCT quantifies and monitors GA progression.
**Fibrotic Scarring**: Chronic CNV can lead to disciform scarring, resulting in permanent vision loss.

sections.title: 11. Red Flags / Emergency Signs
content: **Acute Onset SRF/IRF with Sudden Vision Loss**: Highly suggestive of active neovascular AMD or acute RVO, requiring urgent evaluation and potential anti-VEGF therapy.
**New or Enlarging PED**: Can indicate active CNV, especially if associated with subretinal hyperreflective material or fluid. Fibrovascular PEDs carry high risk.
**Retinal Hemorrhage on OCT**: Suggests active vascular leakage, neovascularization, or severe RVO.
**Full-Thickness Macular Hole**: Requires prompt referral for surgical evaluation (vitrectomy with ILM peel).
**Vitreous Hemorrhage (obscuring OCT view)**: Indicates severe neovascularization (DR, RVO, nAMD) and may require B-scan ultrasound, urgent referral.

sections.title: 13. Key Clinical Pearls for Residents/Fellows
content: **EZ Integrity is Paramount**: The ellipsoid zone (EZ) is the most critical prognostic biomarker for visual acuity. Its disruption usually signifies irreversible photoreceptor damage.
**DRIL = Bad News**: Disorganization of Retinal Inner Layers (DRIL) consistently predicts poor visual outcomes in macular edema, even after fluid resolution.

**Not All Fluid is Equal**: While IRF and SRF are generally bad, the *type* of PED (serous vs. fibrovascular vs. drusenoid) and its characteristics (e.g., notch) are crucial for diagnosis and prognosis.
**HRF ≠ Always Exudates**: Hyperreflective foci can be lipid exudates, activated microglia, or migrating RPE cells. Context is key!
**OCTA for Neovascularization**: Always consider OCTA if CNV is suspected, as it's non-invasive and often superior to FFA for detecting Type 1 CNV or differentiating PCV.
**Trend Analysis**: Don't just look at one scan. Compare serial OCTs to assess stability, progression, or treatment response. Quantitative maps (thickness, volume) are invaluable.

sections.title: 14. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: **Artificial Intelligence (AI) & Machine Learning**: Automated detection, quantification, and prognostication of OCT biomarkers (e.g., fluid volume, GA progression, DRIL) with high accuracy. Examples: DeepMind's AI for AMD/DME, various commercial platforms.

**Novel Anti-VEGF Agents**: Brolucizumab (HAWK/HARRIER) and Faricimab (TENAYA/LUCERNE, YOSEMITE/RHINE) offer extended durability, with OCT fluid resolution as primary endpoint. Faricimab targets Ang-2 in addition to VEGF-A.
**Gene Therapy**: Luxturna (voretigene neparvovec) for RPE65-mediated IRD, with OCT showing improvement in retinal structure and function. Ongoing trials for AMD/DME targeting VEGF expression.
**Quantitative Biomarkers**: Focus on volumetric analysis of fluid, drusen, and GA for more precise monitoring and clinical trial endpoints.
**SS-OCT & Wider Field OCTA**: Improved visualization of choroidal structures, deeper penetration, and wider field-of-view for comprehensive assessment of peripheral lesions and vascular networks.

sections.title: 15. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
content: **Challenges**: Patient cooperation, need for sedation in younger children, smaller eye size, different normative databases.

**Key Applications**: Evaluating retinal development, inherited retinal dystrophies (e.g., Leber congenital amaurosis, Stargardt disease), ROP (retinopathy of prematurity), Coats disease, optic nerve hypoplasia, papilledema.
**Specific Biomarkers**: Macular thickness, foveal contour, outer retinal layer integrity, presence of schisis, cysts, or subretinal fluid are assessed for pediatric conditions.
